identity.real_world_identity_notes: GT1 car built for Le Mans around a twin-turbo 3.5 litre V8, with the road-going homologation special sharing its name. Power reaches the rear wheels through an Xtrac six-speed sequential gearbox worked by a short-throw gear lever, which matches the sequential stick seen in the cockpit rather than paddles.

wheel_rim.notes: Observed from the cockpit during the guided drive.

notes: Simulator behavior was directly observed in a guided drive with automatic clutch and shifting disabled.
The clutch is required to move off, and the gear lever is a sequential stick rather than paddles.

No throttle lift is required on upshifts because a full-throttle clutchless upshift was accepted with automatic cut detected. No automatic blip was detected, so the driver supplies the downshift blip, matching the curated convention for a sequential stick without automatic blip.
'Nissan R390 GT1 - Low Downforce' inherits these verified base controls as an approved aero-package assumption and was not separately live-tested.
Observed live in AMS2 1.6.9.91 via guided verification observation ams2.nissan-r390-gt1.20260813t195441014z-0cff25f1 by Jason Kinslow.

confidence.basis: Simulator behavior was live-tested in AMS2 1.6.9.91 with automatic clutch and shifting disabled, and the Xtrac six-speed sequential with a lever is supported by a registered secondary source.

notes: Observed live in AC 14923034 via guided verification observation ac.lmgt-nisumo-r39-v8.20260822t172507073z-bf9e2791 by Jason Kinslow.

overrides.condition: The fingerprinted RSS v2 implementation accepted the tested clutchless coast downshift without driver throttle input and supplied an automatic throttle blip.

confidence.basis: The guided coast-downshift test directly observed acceptance without a driver blip.

overrides.condition: The fingerprinted RSS v2 implementation produced a throttle spike during the accepted clutchless downshift while automatic throttle blip was disabled in the assist settings.

confidence.basis: The guided drive directly detected the automatic throttle spike with the driver-assist setting disabled.

overrides.condition: The fingerprinted RSS v2 cockpit depicts a D-shaped rim instead of the round rim carried by the curated car and AMS2 implementation.

confidence.basis: The cockpit rim was directly inspected during the guided drive.

overrides.condition: The fingerprinted RSS v2 cockpit depicts no wheel-mounted shift lights, while the curated car and AMS2 implementation carry them.

confidence.basis: Wheel-mounted shift-light equipment was directly inspected during the guided drive.

RSS's first-party pack documentation and installed metadata identify the exact fingerprinted implementation as the primarily-1998 long-tail, 3,495 cc twin-turbo V8 car. NISMO independently gives that same combination only to the 1998 R390 GT1 and records its sequential transmission. Six sequential-stick gears, clutch-required move-off, automatic cut/blip, and cockpit wheel equipment were directly observed.

claims.basis: A registered secondary source establishes the 1998 GT1 identity and its Xtrac sequential gearbox, and the exact simulator identity was observed live.
The source specifies an Xtrac six-speed sequential operated by a short-throw lever, and the live drive confirmed six gears through a sequential stick.
Directly observed during the guided drive: move-off, shift clutch use, automatic cut and blip, and the cockpit rim.
The drive accepted a full-throttle clutchless upshift with automatic cut, so no lift is required, and detected no automatic blip on downshifts, so the driver supplies the rev-matching blip.

RSS Classic Endurance Pack 1 readme, PDF/printed page 3, says the Nisumo R39 was built for 1997 and 1998, depicts the long-tail used primarily in 1998, and uses a 3,495 cc twin-turbo V8. NISMO's own history says the 1998 Nissan R390 GT1 became a long-tail and changed to a Nissan-built sequential transmission. The year, body revision, displacement, engine layout, aspiration, category and fictionalized model token converge on the existing 1998 R390 GT1 record rather than a neighboring Nissan prototype.
